questions.question: Set out how the free market and the centrally planned economy each answer the three economic questions, and give one strength and one weakness of each system with its mechanism spelled out.
questions.expected_answer: In the free market, WHAT is decided by consumers spending their income — consumer sovereignty, every rand a ballot; HOW is decided by producers hunting the least-cost mix of labour and machinery; FOR WHOM is decided by income, so output flows to purchasing power. A strength is efficiency with innovation: producers who waste resources make losses and vanish, while new products win profit, and the system adjusts to changed wants without any committee. A weakness is inequality plus market failure, stated as mechanisms: because for whom is settled by ability to pay, a person born without assets or schooling receives almost nothing; public goods like lighthouses and police patrols are non-excludable so nobody pays voluntarily and they are under-supplied; and a polluting smelter pays nothing for the harm it causes, so its output is too large. In the centrally planned economy, one body answers all three questions: the planning authority decides what according to its reading of social need, the plan assigns each enterprise its workers, machines and materials, and the state distributes through set wages, rations and subsidised services. A strength is that resources can be swung rapidly behind one national goal and basic needs guaranteed regardless of earnings. The central weakness is the information problem: no office can collect the millions of local facts that market prices summarise automatically, so plans are always partly wrong, and because administered prices cannot move, the errors persist as queues for some goods and warehouses of others.

questions.question: Define a mixed economy, show how it divides the answers to the three questions, and name the South African institutions and policies that make South Africa one.
questions.expected_answer: A mixed economy combines private ownership, enterprise and market prices with state ownership, regulation and provision. WHAT is decided mainly by consumers through markets, with government filling the market's blind spots by supplying public goods such as roads, courts and policing and merit goods such as basic schooling and clinics. HOW is decided by firms pursuing least cost inside a fence of rules — labour law, environmental standards, competition law and safety codes. FOR WHOM starts with income earned in the market and is then modified by redistribution: progressive income tax, social grants, free basic water and electricity, no-fee schools and public health care. South Africa fits closely: the Constitution protects property while entrenching socio-economic rights; private firms produce most output while state-owned enterprises run electricity, rail, harbours, broadcasting and post; regulators such as the Competition Commission, the National Credit Regulator and the energy and communications authorities referee the markets; and progressive taxation funds one of the developing world's largest social grant systems.

questions.question: Explain what it means to call South Africa a DUALISTIC economy and account for the dualism through its structural causes.
questions.expected_answer: Dualism means two economies operate side by side within one country. South Africa's first economy is formal, modern, capital-intensive and globally connected — listed corporations, deep mines, sophisticated banks, commercial agriculture and high-skill services, with written contracts and access to credit. The second economy is informal and survivalist — hawking at taxi ranks, spaza retail, backyard services, subsistence plots and piece work — with tiny capital per worker, no contracts, no formal credit and low productivity. The causes are structural, not personal effort. Generations of land dispossession and the migrant labour system stripped and concentrated ownership, so one side inherited capital and the other nothing to pledge. Apartheid spatial planning settled the majority far from workplaces, so transport devours a large share of small wages. Schooling was engineered to be unequal, withholding the qualifications the formal economy demands. And the collateral wall completes the trap: banks lend against assets, so the assetless cannot borrow the capital that would let them grow. South Africa's mixed-economy policies — land reform, township enterprise finance, no-fee schooling, free basic services and commuter transport — are attempts to cut doors through these walls.
